# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles population estimates for 5.692 towns, ports, fortresses, market towns (*miasteczka*) and factory settlements across the 40 provinces and frontier regions of the Russian Empire and its neighbouring partition lands between the Peace of Nystad (1721AD) and the Congress of Vienna (1815AD). Arranged across the Baltic provinces and Finland, the Polish-Lithuanian partition lands and Galicia, Ukraine and Novorossiya, Central Russia and the Volga-Urals, the Caucasus and Siberia, the tables follow urban growth across five Soul Revision benchmarks (1721, 1762, 1795, 1811 and 1815AD). Over these nine decades, the rapid rise of Saint Petersburg, the founding of new Black Sea ports led by Odessa, Kherson and Sevastopol, the growth of Ural and Altai iron and silver works and the annexation of Polish-Lithuanian market towns reshaped the urban map, even as the 1771AD plague and the 1812AD fire and retreat inflicted sharp losses on Moscow, Smolensk, Vitebsk and Vilna.

# Methodology

This gazetteer presents population estimates for 5.692 towns, fortress settlements, maritime ports, market towns (*miasteczka* or *shtetlekh*), colonist centres, Ural and Altai iron and silver works (*gornye zavody*) and Siberian *ostrogi* across the 40 provinces and frontier regions of Early Imperial Russia and its adjacent partition lands between 1721AD and 1815AD [@Kabuzan1963; @Kabuzan1971; @Vodarsky1973; @Mironov1990Urban]. Across the entire 40-region area (18,5M km²), total population more than doubled from 23,89M in 1721AD to 51,17M in 1815AD (or from 22,26M to 47,82M within the 39 regions belonging to the Russian Empire in 1815AD, excluding Austrian Galicia and Bukovina). Each entry gives the settlement's main name, historical or local names, coordinates and modern country alongside its population at the principal revision benchmarks (1721AD, 1762AD, 1795AD, 1811AD and 1815AD).

Town figures draw on the merchant and townsmen (*posad* and *meshchane*) rolls of the first seven Imperial Soul Revisions (1719-1816AD) together with provincial police and military-statistical returns compiled by Boris Mironov, Yaroslav Vodarsky, Vladimir Kabuzan and Pyotr Keppen [@Mironov1990Urban; @Vodarsky1973; @Kabuzan1990; @Keppen1857]. Outside the Great Russian core, these returns are paired with Baltic German ploughland and Lutheran magistracy lists [@Hupel1774; @Palli1996], Swedish-Finnish *Tabellverket* town registers [@Jutikkala1965; @Turpeinen1979], Polish-Lithuanian hearth-tax (*podymne*) and Jewish *kahal* rolls alongside Austrian Galician conscriptions [@Kuklo2009; @Stampfer1995; @Fellerer2023Galicia], Novorossiya and Bessarabia colonist chancellery tables [@Skalkovsky1836; @Herlihy1986; @Bushin2011; @Feldman2023Bessarabia], Ural and Altai mining-chancellery inventories [@Portal1950; @Smirnov1992UralZavody; @Isaev2025AltaiCabinet] and Siberian post-road and *ostrog* returns [@Hartley2014; @Forsyth1992]. Ports, fortresses and factory towns founded after 1721AD - such as Ekaterinburg (1723AD), Orenburg (1735/1743AD), Barnaul (1730s), Petropavlovsk-Kamchatsky (1740AD), Elisavetgrad (1754AD), Izhevsk (1760AD), Katharinenstadt (1765AD), Kherson (1778AD), Mariupol (1778AD), Sevastopol (1783AD), Simferopol (1784AD), Nikolaev (1789AD), Ekaterinodar (1793AD), Odessa (1794AD) and Novocherkassk (1805AD) - show a hyphen (-) before their foundation and New in the percentage change column.

## Grodno Governorate & Belostok Oblast

Table \ref{tab:reg7-sites} lists the towns of Region 7 (Grodno Governorate and Belostok Oblast, 40,42k km²), where regional population rose from 360k in 1721AD to 760k in 1811AD before dropping to 695k in 1815AD (+93,1%) [@Kuklo2009; @Reutskaya2016Belarus; @Klier1986].

## Minsk Governorate & Polesia

## Sloboda-Ukrainian (Kharkov Governorate)

## Taurida Governorate (Crimea)

Table \ref{tab:reg17-sites} lists the towns of Region 17 (Taurida Governorate, 69,87k km²), where regional population stood at 370k in 1721AD, dipped after the 1783AD annexation and returned to 345k in 1811AD and 370k in 1815AD (0% net change) [@Williams2001; @Dmitriev2018CrimeaEmigration; @Kabuzan1976Novorossiya].

## Arkhangelsk & Vologda Governorates

Table \ref{tab:reg21-sites} lists the towns of Region 21 (Arkhangelsk and Vologda Governorates, 1,31M km²), where regional population rose from 560k in 1721AD to 905k in 1811AD and 920k in 1815AD (+64,3%) [@Vodarsky1977; @Kabuzan1971; @Kahan1985].

## Moscow Governorate

Table \ref{tab:reg22-sites} lists the towns of Region 22 (Moscow Governorate, 28,08k km²), where regional population rose from 725k in 1721AD to 1,24M in 1811AD before falling to 1,12M in 1815AD (+54,5%) [@Alexander1980; @Iskhakov2013Plague1771; @Mironov1990Urban; @Lieven2009].

## Smolensk, Kaluga & Tver Governorates

Table \ref{tab:reg23-sites} lists the towns of Region 23 (Smolensk, Kaluga and Tver Governorates, 152,78k km²), where regional population grew from 1,72M in 1721AD to 2,87M in 1811AD before dropping to 2,64M in 1815AD (+53,5%) [@Shelomentseva2015Smolensk1812; @Lieven2009; @Mironov1990Urban].

## Lower Volga: Saratov & Astrakhan

Table \ref{tab:reg28-sites} lists the towns of Region 28 (Saratov and Astrakhan Governorates, 329,07k km²), where regional population grew from 480k in 1721AD to 1,49M in 1811AD and 1,58M in 1815AD (+229,2%) [@Bartlett1979; @Galperina2013VolgaGermans; @Khodarkovsky1992; @Ochirov2012Kalmyk1771].

## Province of the Don Cossack Host

Table \ref{tab:reg29-sites} lists the towns of Region 29 (Province of the Don Cossack Host, 172,66k km²), where regional population rose from 180k in 1721AD to 645k in 1811AD and 680k in 1815AD (+277,8%) [@Sunderland2004; @Kabuzan1971; @Mironov1990Urban].

## North Caucasian Highlanders

Table \ref{tab:reg31-sites} lists the principal settlements of Region 31 (North Caucasian Highlands: Circassia, Kabarda, Chechnya and Dagestan, 149,43k km²), where regional population rose from 780k in 1721AD to 905k in 1811AD and 910k in 1815AD (+16,7%) [@Tovsultanov2017; @Kabuzan1990; @Kappeler2001].

## Tobolsk South: Siberian Trakt & Ishim

## Tobolsk North: Ob-Irtysh Basin

Table \ref{tab:reg35-sites} lists the towns and *ostrogi* of Region 35 (Northern Tobolsk and the Ob-Irtysh basin, 1,64M km²), where regional population rose from 85k in 1721AD to 156k in 1811AD and 160k in 1815AD (+88,2%) [@Forsyth1992; @Korusenko2011Siberia; @Hartley2014].

## Tomsk & Altai Silver Mines

Table \ref{tab:reg36-sites} lists the towns and mining settlements of Region 36 (Tomsk Governorate and the Altai Cabinet silver district, 499,97k km²), where regional population grew from 95k in 1721AD to 289k in 1811AD and 300k in 1815AD (+215,8%) [@Isaev2025AltaiCabinet; @Hartley2014; @Kahan1985].
